questions.question: What is the main goal of a commitment scheme?
options: Let someone publish a value now and reveal it later, while preventing changes in-between
Let two parties exchange keys without revealing the keys to eavesdroppers
Let someone encrypt a message so only the receiver can read it
Let someone prove they know a secret without revealing any information at all
questions.explanation: A commitment is a two-phase protocol: commit now (hide the value), open later (bind you to that value).

questions.question: In a group of order q, what does it mean for an exponent to live in Z_q?
options: Exponents are interpreted modulo q
Exponents must be prime numbers less than q
Exponents are interpreted modulo p for some prime p
Exponents must be non-negative integers with no wraparound
questions.explanation: Working in Z_q means you reduce exponents modulo q, so values wrap around at q.

questions.question: In multiplicative notation, what is a Pedersen commitment to message m with blinding r?
options: C = g^m · h^r
C = g^(m·r)
C = H(m || r)
C = g^r · h^m · (m + r)
questions.explanation: Pedersen’s commit is C = g^m h^r in a prime-order cyclic group with public generators g and h.

questions.question: Why is Pedersen commitment perfectly hiding when r is uniform in Z_q (in a prime-order group)?
options: Because h^r is uniform over the group, making C independent of m
Because discrete log is hard, so m cannot be recovered
Because g is secret and never revealed
Because the verifier checks a hash of (m, r) instead of C
questions.explanation: Perfect hiding is information-theoretic: uniform r makes h^r uniform, so C reveals no information about m.

questions.question: If C1 = Commit(m1, r1) and C2 = Commit(m2, r2) use the same parameters, what does C1 · C2 commit to?
options: (m1 + m2 mod q, r1 + r2 mod q)
(m1 · m2 mod q, r1 · r2 mod q)
(m1 − m2 mod q, r1 − r2 mod q)
questions.explanation: Pedersen commitments are additively homomorphic: multiplying commitments adds messages and blindings modulo q.

questions.question: What goes wrong if the party choosing parameters knows α such that h = g^α (i.e., log_g(h))?
options: They can forge openings and claim the same commitment is to any message they want
They can recover m from C without the opening
They can make commitments that cannot be verified by anyone
Nothing goes wrong; α is always safe to publish alongside parameters
questions.explanation: Knowing α breaks binding for that party: they can adjust r to open the same C to a different m.

questions.question: When using a prime-order subgroup of Z_p* of order q, which check helps ensure a received element C is in the subgroup?
options: 0 < C < p and C^q ≡ 1 (mod p)
C is even
C has at most q bits
C^p ≡ 1 (mod q)
questions.explanation: Subgroup membership checks prevent small-subgroup and invalid-element issues in protocols built on commitments.

questions.question: Why do systems that commit to amounts (e.g., balances) typically require a range proof in addition to a Pedersen commitment?
options: Because commitments are modulo q, so without constraints the committer could encode negative/overflow values
Because Pedersen commitments cannot be verified without a signature
Because Pedersen commitments leak the message unless m is a hash output
Because range proofs are needed to make commitments deterministic
questions.explanation: A Pedersen commitment binds only to an exponent in Z_q; range proofs enforce that the intended integer lies in a safe interval.
